title: Rudolf Blaschka 1892 — collection-aware field filtering and negative-evidence discipline

direct_evidence: Rudolf says season itself limits the available selection.
He says Cambridge is 'picky' and does not want certain species because they are already represented.
He reports 200 species drawn and studied to date and estimates 400 by departure.
He says 600-800 would require wandering America for an entire year, which he explicitly rejects.
He contrasts wild collecting with botanical-garden access, where names and other identifying information are already at hand.

main_result: Field yield was collection-aware before material returned to Cambridge. Harvard's existing collection operated as a remote negative selector: a plant could be locally available and botanically interesting yet excluded because the receiving collection already represented it.
revised_selection_model: maker's judgment of interest or characteristic form
Cambridge collection-state test: already represented or still lacking
feasible reference medium: drawing, dried specimen, alcohol, seed, bulb, live plant, later supply
formula: field reference yield = availability × maker selection × collection gap × media feasibility × bodily/time/route capacity
historical_implication: The expedition was not autonomous field collecting followed by downstream institutional acceptance. Collection development reached upstream into field practice. Cambridge's inventory shaped what Rudolf considered worth recording while he was still travelling.
negative_evidence_rule: The current sources identify the filtering mechanism but do not yet name individual species explicitly rejected by Cambridge as 'already represented'. Do not manufacture a rejected-taxon list from later absences or same-genus matches.

relation_to_yield_counts: Rudolf's 200 and projected 400 are not raw encounter totals. They sit downstream from environmental availability, collection-state filtering and his own working capacity. They should remain in the 'drawn/studied or projected retained reference' family rather than being called species encountered or collected without qualification.
